title: Legendary Pawn
reviewNotes: Complete seven-piece 26-second ...Rxf1 diagram reviewed: White Ke6/Rh2/g4 versus Black Kh6/Rf1/Bh5/h7. Drawing practice goal, source Rxh5+/Kg6 and independent losing g5+/Kg6 all checked. The g4 pawn protects Rh5. Earlier nine-piece Rf2 attack, eight-piece g4 mistake and separate Be2 sacrifice remain outside proof.
transcript: White has a brilliant idea. The material is even, but the rook to F2 sets up a checkmate in one threat. There is no way for this rook to stop the threat, but the bishop can come to D1. And now, after rook to H2 check, the bishop can cover like this. Now, some of you might think that the idea is to play G4 and add pressure to this bishop, but unfortunately, this gives away the win. After rook to F3 check, black is going to pick up this bishop, and even if we take the bishop with check, this is a textbook draw. There is no way to make progress. Both sides have a rook and a pawn left. So, in this position, white has to find a brilliant idea, a beautiful sacrifice with bishop to E2. This move does a bunch of things at the same time. First of all, it adds pressure to the bishop and threatens to take it on the next move. It defends the F3 square from the rook check, and it's trying to distract this black rook >> [music] >> and to bait it into taking. Now, the rooks see each other, but if we take here, the bishop is unpinned, and we're actually losing the game. So, was that just a blunder? Did white give away a piece for nothing? Well, not exactly, because here's the follow-up. G4, sacrificing the rook completely and threatening to [music] take like this, this time with a checkmate. There is no rook check because our rook is covering that. But of course, black can take the rook, but once he does that, with only a pawn left, pawn to G5 is an incredible checkmate.
